newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bund futures hit by fears of higher U.S. rates.
newsitem.headline: Bund futures hit by fears of higher U.S. rates.

text.p: Bund futures tumbled in late trade, but outperformed their U.S. counterparts, after Federal Reserve Board chairman Alan Greenspan said he could not rule out a pre-emptive tightening of interest rates.

Bunds, which had traded in negative territory much of the day ahead of Greenspan's remarks, slid as low as 102.86, but quickly recovered somewhat to trade above the psychologically important 103.00 level.
At 1524 GMT, the March DTB Bund futures contract was down 25 basis points at 103.09.
Bunds hammered Treasuries on Greenspan's remarks, pushing the spread back toward historic highs at 103 basis points from 93 basis points at the previous close.

"It should not be too surprising that Bunds have so strongly outperformed," said Stuart Trow, manager of market analysis at Norinchukin Int'l Plc. "German interest rates are not going up and may even go down."
He said Bunds' outperformance could be most pronounced on the short end of the yield between two- and five-year maturities.

Some analysts figure the T-note/Bund spread could widen out to around 120 basis points over the next several months. The 103 basis point difference seen today was only the second time it had topped over 100 this year.

Analysts said that with the Greenspan remarks out of the way, Bunds and debt markets may recover somewhat and that the contract's 102.86 low could mark the bottom of a trading range that could last a week or so.
But others remained on guard. "This is the second time that Greenspan has wagged his finger," one trader said referring to the Fed chairman's remarks from late last year.
"The second time that he wags his finger something is in the pipeline," he said. Analysts said they thought the German yield curve may flatten in the wake of Greenspan's remarks.

The short end of the curve is likely to remain focused on domestic factors which are likely to be Bund market supportive, while the longer end may focus on international issues such as the chances of higher U.S. interest rates, one said.
The deputy president of the Bundesbank, Johann Wilhelm Gaddum, said in an interview conducted on February 18 but not published until today that he did not see grounds for a rate cut.
The next factor likely to catch the market's attention will be a speech by Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer on Thursday morning at 0945 GMT in Frankfurt.
With worries about a timely start of European monetary union mounting, even the usual comments about strictly following Maastricht guidelines could carry added weight.
